title: Dream and Angel Reese Lead Atlanta to First WNBA Finals Since 2013, Sweeping Liberty
body:
Atlanta’s women’s basketball team clinched a berth in the WNBA Finals for the first time in 13 years, edging the New York Liberty 85‑83 in a dramatic Game 3 that completed a 3‑0 sweep of the Eastern Conference semifinals. The decisive victory, secured on the road, was propelled by a late‑stage surge from Angel Reese and a steady hand from point guard Jordin Canada, who together turned a tightly contested matchup into a showcase of the Dream’s resurgence.

The series began with New York taking a 2‑1 lead after a high‑scoring Game 2, but Atlanta refused to bow out. In the final showdown, the Dream built a modest lead early, only to see the Liberty claw back and tie the game at 71‑71 midway through the fourth quarter. Reese, who had been quiet for much of the night, exploded in the closing minutes, scoring eight of her 19 points after the 71‑71 tie and converting a clutch three‑pointer that gave Atlanta a two‑point cushion with 1:12 remaining. Canada, the league’s leading assist provider, orchestrated the offense throughout, finishing with 13 points, 10 assists and a crucial steal that set up the final bucket.

Reese’s performance was emblematic of a broader shift in the Dream’s identity. Drafted second overall in 2023, the 22‑year‑old forward has quickly become a fan favorite for her tenacity and scoring versatility. Her ability to dominate the paint against a Liberty frontcourt anchored by veteran center Sabrina Ionescu highlighted the Dream’s interior advantage. Meanwhile, Canada’s poise under pressure reaffirmed her status as the team’s engine. Her 10‑assist night marked the third consecutive playoff game in which she has facilitated at least double‑digit assists, underscoring the Dream’s reliance on a balanced, ball‑movement offense.

The sweep also marked a significant milestone for head coach Tanisha Wright, who has guided Atlanta from a rebuilding phase to championship contention in just two seasons. Wright’s strategic adjustments—particularly the decision to employ a high‑low set that allowed Reese to operate near the rim while Canada penetrated and kicked out—proved decisive. The coaching staff’s emphasis on defensive intensity paid dividends as well; the Dream forced 18 turnovers in the series, converting them into fast‑break points that kept the Liberty off balance.

For the Liberty, the loss was a painful reminder of the fine margins that separate victory from defeat in postseason play. New York’s star guard Sabrina Ionescu posted 23 points and 11 assists, but missed several critical free throws in the final minute that could have swung the outcome. The team will now turn its attention to the offseason, where roster moves and the upcoming draft will be crucial to re‑establishing its status as a contender.

Looking ahead, Atlanta’s path to the championship will pit them against the Western Conference champion, a team that has displayed both depth and experience throughout the playoffs. The Dream’s blend of youthful exuberance and seasoned leadership suggests they are well‑positioned to challenge for the title, but they will need to maintain the composure that carried them past New York and continue to execute in clutch moments. As the franchise celebrates its first Finals appearance since 2013, the city of Atlanta can anticipate a historic run that could culminate in a long‑awaited championship, reigniting passion for women’s basketball across the region.
